papers.summary: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.

papers.title: Toward Verifiable Auto-Research for Data Systems
papers.authors: Kaiwen Zheng, Srijan Srivastava, Zheng Yan, Xinpeng Zhao et al.
papers.what: [Explore] AI auto-research is poised to forge bespoke data systems, from key-value stores and indexes to query engines, each engineered for a specific workload and hardware platform. Yet this promise rests on fragile ground. An agent optimizes what it can measure, not necessarily what user
papers.summary: AI auto-research is poised to forge bespoke data systems, from key-value stores and indexes to query engines, each engineered for a specific workload and hardware platform. Yet this promise rests on fragile ground. An agent optimizes what it can measure, not necessarily what users need. Natural-language requirements leave ample room for specification gaming, producing systems that blaze through benchmarks while silently losing updates or violating consistency. Worse, each research iteration consumes tokens, while validating a candidate under real concurrency, memory pressure, and failure conditions can stretch the entire research process into weeks. In this paper, we envision a more cost-efficient and verifiable approach to auto-research. Precise and composable specifications anchor the search, lightweight performance critics prune costly dead ends, and falsification and deductive verification make correctness an integral part of the process rather than an afterthought. By treating correctness, performance, research time, and token cost as equally important objectives, we aim to transform AI-generated data systems from plausible artifacts into trustworthy, production-grade systems whose behavior can be understood, audited, and ultimately relied upon.

papers.title: ARoute: Task-Aligned Batch and Streaming Model Routing
papers.authors: Daofu Zhang, Qingcheng Zeng, Chunwei Liu, Fuheng Zhao
papers.what: [Explore] Language models increasingly power data-intensive applications, from semantic data processing to question answering and agentic workflows. Using frontier models for every request is prohibitively expensive, while relying only on smaller models reduces accuracy. We study model rou
papers.summary: Language models increasingly power data-intensive applications, from semantic data processing to question answering and agentic workflows. Using frontier models for every request is prohibitively expensive, while relying only on smaller models reduces accuracy. We study model routing under a user-specified cost budget, aiming to maximize accuracy under task-specific correctness criteria. Existing routers fall short in two ways: pretrained routers rely on generic preference signals that may not reflect a task's own correctness criteria or a new model pair, and model cascades run the weaker model first on every request, adding sequential latency. We present ARoute, a task-aligned router that learns cost and accuracy signals to select a model for each request before inference. ARoute has two variants: ARoute-Batch operates on a batch of requests known in advance, routing requests with the greatest expected benefit to the stronger model subject to the budget, whereas ARoute-Stream processes requests online, using a threshold calibrated on a small validation set to satisfy the cost quota and dynamically adjusting it as the budget is consumed. For ARoute-Stream, we provide a finite-sample guarantee on expected normalized spending. We evaluate ARoute on MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, SuperGPQA, and two value-filling tasks built from SWAN semantic query benchmark against other state-of-the-art approaches. At matched cost, ARoute-Batch achieves the highest mean accuracy in all 15 task-cost settings, improving over the strongest baseline by 4.1 percentage points on average and by up to 11.9 points. ARoute also completes a batch up to 2.8x faster than cascades.

papers.title: Testing Conditional Moment Restrictions in Networks
papers.authors: Wenxuan Ding
papers.what: [Explore] Parametric models of network formation, such as dyadic logit models, are increasingly popular, but few tools exist to test their specification. This paper develops a specification test for conditionally independent dyad (CID) models based on the probabilities that these models as
papers.summary: Parametric models of network formation, such as dyadic logit models, are increasingly popular, but few tools exist to test their specification. This paper develops a specification test for conditionally independent dyad (CID) models based on the probabilities that these models assign to subgraphs, the patterns of links among small groups of agents. Given the agents' characteristics, a parametric CID model determines not only the probability of each link but also the probability that a group of agents forms a triangle, a star, or any other subgraph. Under correct specification, the expected frequency of each subgraph among agents with given characteristics equals its model-implied probability. This forms the basis of the testable conditional moment restrictions. The test statistic is the weighted integrated squared distance between a nonparametric kernel estimate of these probabilities and the probabilities implied by the estimated parametric model. I derive its asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis.
